answerSnippet: The flexitarian diet uses a 20/30/50 macro split: 20% of calories from protein, 30% from fat, and 50% from carbs. For 2,000 kcal/day that means 100 g protein, 67 g fat, and 250 g carbs. The weekly structure is 5 plant-based days (legumes, tofu, eggs) + 2 days with meat or fish.

intro: The **flexitarian diet** (coined by Dawn Jackson Blatner, 2009) is essentially vegetarian with strategic exceptions: **5 plant-based days per week + 2 days with fish or poultry**. The standard macro split is **20% protein / 30% fat / 50% carbohydrates**. Ranked #2 in US News Best Diets 2024 and #1 in sustainable diets, it delivers cardiovascular benefits and a 25% reduction in carbon footprint—without the strictness of veganism. This calculator gives you your exact daily macro targets and a 7-day protein plan.
keyTakeaway: Flexitarian split: **20% protein + 30% fat + 50% carbs**. For 2,000 kcal: 100 g protein, 67 g fat, 250 g carbs. 5 plant-based + 2 meat/fish days per week.

explanation:
## How the flexitarian macro formula works

The 20/30/50 macro split is the canonical Blatner flexitarian distribution:

```
protein (g) = daily_kcal × 0.20 / 4
fat (g)     = daily_kcal × 0.30 / 9
carbs (g)   = daily_kcal × 0.50 / 4
```

Protein (1 gram = 4 kcal) and carbs (1 gram = 4 kcal) both yield 4 kcal per gram; fat (1 gram = 9 kcal) is more calorie-dense.

## Flexitarian macro reference table

| Calories/day | Protein (g) | Fat (g) | Carbs (g) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1,600 | 80 | 53 | 200 |
| 1,800 | 90 | 60 | 225 |
| 2,000 | 100 | 67 | 250 |
| 2,200 | 110 | 73 | 275 |
| 2,500 | 125 | 83 | 313 |
| 2,800 | 140 | 93 | 350 |
| 3,000 | 150 | 100 | 375 |

Values aligned with Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics flexitarian position paper (2023) and EAT-Lancet reference diet.

## 7-day protein source plan

| Day | Plant-based protein source | Meat/fish? |
|---|---|---|
| Monday | Lentils + rice (completes all amino acids) | No |
| Tuesday | Tofu or tempeh stir-fry | No |
| Wednesday | Salmon or tuna (150 g) | Yes |
| Thursday | Chickpeas + eggs | No |
| Friday | Chicken breast (150 g) or sardines | Yes |
| Saturday | Edamame + quinoa | No |
| Sunday | Eggs + cheese + legume soup | No |

## Blatner levels

| Level | Meat servings/week |
|---|---|
| Beginner | 6–8 (about 100 g each) |
| Advanced | 3–4 |
| Expert | 0–2 |

## Key nutrients to watch

- **Vitamin B12**: zero in plant foods — supplement 250 μg/day or 2,500 μg/week.
- **Iron and zinc**: absorption from legumes improves with vitamin C at the same meal.
- **Omega-3 (EPA/DHA)**: include flaxseed/chia oil, or algae oil supplement on plant days.
- **Calcium**: fortified plant milk or broccoli + almonds on veggie days.

## Special cases

- **Athletes on flexitarian**: bump protein target to 1.4–1.8 g/kg body weight on training days.
- **Weight loss**: reduce total calories 15% and raise protein share to 25% to preserve muscle.
- **Type 2 diabetes**: favor low-GI plant days (lentils, chickpeas over rice); lean meat only.

## Common mistakes

1. Relying on ultra-processed plant burgers — high in sodium and saturated fat.
2. Skipping B12 supplementation on plant-heavy weeks.
3. Under-eating protein on plant days (aim 25–30 g per meal).
4. Treating meat days as unlimited cheat days — portion control still applies.

## Sources

Evidence from Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, EAT-Lancet Commission (Willett et al. 2019), and Blatner (2009).

## Editorial review

**Reviewed by the Hacé Cuentas editorial team.** Each reference value is cross-checked against the cited official sources. Results are informational — not a replacement for personalized medical or dietitian advice.

faq.q: What macros should I eat on a flexitarian diet?
faq.a: The standard flexitarian macro split is **20% protein, 30% fat, 50% carbohydrates**. For 2,000 kcal/day that works out to 100 g protein, 67 g fat, and 250 g carbs. This is the canonical Blatner distribution, designed to support mostly plant-based eating while allowing occasional meat.

faq.q: How many grams of protein do I need on flexitarian diet?
faq.a: At 20% of calories: **1,800 kcal → 90 g protein; 2,000 kcal → 100 g; 2,500 kcal → 125 g**. Athletes should target 1.4–1.8 g per kg of body weight and may need to bump protein percentage to 25% on training days.

A mostly plant-based eating pattern with strategic meat or fish on 2 days per week. Coined by dietitian Dawn Jackson Blatner in 2009. It's flexible vegetarianism—you reduce meat dramatically without eliminating it. Macro split: 20% protein, 30% fat, 50% carbs.

faq.q: How many days per week can I eat meat on flexitarian?
faq.a: The flexitarian structure calls for **5 plant-based days + 2 days with fish or poultry**. Beginners can start with 2–3 plant-based days and work up. Expert level reaches 0–2 meat servings per week total.

faq.q: How much weight can I lose on a flexitarian diet?
faq.a: Average weight loss is **4–6 kg (9–13 lbs) over 6 months**, according to studies comparing flexitarians to omnivores on similar calorie deficits. The high fiber from plant foods increases satiety, helping maintain the deficit naturally.

faq.q: Does a flexitarian diet reduce carbon footprint?
faq.a: Yes — approximately **25% lower carbon footprint** compared to a meat-heavy omnivorous diet, according to Poore & Nemecek (2018, Science). Shifting even 5 days per week away from meat accounts for most of the environmental gain.

faq.q: Is the flexitarian diet the same as pescatarian?
faq.a: No. Pescatarian means no meat but fish is always allowed. Flexitarian means mostly plant-based with *occasional* poultry, beef, or fish — maximum flexibility on which protein you choose when you do eat animal products.

faq.q: Do I need to take supplements on a flexitarian diet?
faq.a: **Vitamin B12** is the main one — supplement 250 μg/day or 2,500 μg/week if your plant-based days outnumber your meat days. Omega-3 (algae oil) on plant days is also recommended. Iron and zinc from legumes are adequate with proper food combining (add vitamin C at the same meal).

faq.q: Can athletes follow a flexitarian diet and build muscle?
faq.a: Yes, with adjustments. Increase protein to 1.4–1.8 g/kg body weight on training days, prioritize post-workout plant proteins (pea + rice protein blend), and supplement B12 weekly. The 2 meat/fish days provide full amino acid profiles to complement plant sources.

faq.q: How does the flexitarian diet reduce heart disease risk?
faq.a: Research shows a **15% reduction in cardiovascular mortality** for flexitarian eaters. The mechanism: high fiber from plant days lowers LDL cholesterol, omega-3 from fish days reduces triglycerides, and reduced red meat lowers saturated fat intake — a triple cardiovascular benefit.
